Day 1
From Hotel: 11 min · 4 min → Al-Qarawiyyin Mosque and University
1.Al-Qarawiyyin Mosque and University
Founded in 857–859 by Fatima al-Fihri, Al-Qarawiyyin is recognized as the oldest continuously operating institution of higher education in the world; non-Muslims can't enter the prayer hall but can view the tiled courtyard and fountains through the main gate on Derb Boutouil.

4 min · 3 min → Nejjarine Museum of Wooden Arts and Crafts
2.Nejjarine Museum of Wooden Arts and Crafts
Built in 1711 as a funduq — a merchants' inn and storehouse arranged around a courtyard — the building now holds three floors of carved wooden crafts behind one of the medina's most ornamental gateways, beside the equally decorated Nejjarine Fountain.

3.Dar Batha Museum
A former royal palace commissioned by Sultan Hassan I in the late 19th century, now the Al Batha Museum of Islamic Arts, with over 6,500 objects of ceramics, woodwork, textiles and traditional crafts set around a shaded Andalusian garden.

21 min · 8 min → Chouara Tannery
4.Chouara Tannery
The largest and oldest of Fez's three tanneries, a grid of round stone vessels filled with dye and softening liquid, worked in the same manner since the medieval city's founding; leather-shop terraces around Tannery Square give the classic overhead view.

Day 2
From Hotel: 26 min · 10 min → Bab Boujloud
1.Bab Boujloud
The blue-and-green tiled Blue Gate is the ceremonial entrance to Fes el-Bali — blue for the city on the outward face, green for Islam on the face turned toward the medina.
Read more
Open 24/7
~15 min
Place Bou Jeloud · Fes El Bali
2 min · 3 min → Dar al-Magana
2.Dar al-Magana
A 14th-century weight-powered water clock designed for Sultan Abu Inan Faris by the astronomer Abu'l-Hassan Ali — thirteen carved cedar beams and twelve arched windows survive on the facade opposite Bou Inania Madrasa, once fitted with brass bowls that rang the hours.
Read more
Open 24/7
~10 min
Rue Talaa Sghira · Fes El Bali
1 min · 3 min → Bou Inania Madrasa
3.Bou Inania Madrasa
Built in 1350–55 by the Marinid sultan Abu Inan Faris, this is the only madrasa in Morocco that also functioned as a congregational mosque, with a minaret and a wide prayer hall behind a courtyard of carved cedar and zellij tilework.

11 min · 4 min → Jnan Sbil Gardens
4.Jnan Sbil Gardens
Laid out in the 19th century by Sultan Moulay Hassan I and fully reopened to the public in 1917, this 7.5-hectare garden between Fes el-Bali and Fes el-Jdid holds ponds, Moorish water features and over 3,000 plant species — a shaded, quiet close to a day of walking.

Day 3
From Hotel: 12 min → Borj Nord
1.Borj Nord
Built in 1582 by the Saadi sultan Ahmad al-Mansour and modeled on Portuguese forts, this hilltop bastion now houses the Museum of Arms — a collection of Moroccan and international weaponry inside thick fortified walls with sweeping views over the medina.

15 min · 6 min → Marinid Tombs
2.Marinid Tombs
The ruined 14th-century royal necropolis of the Marinid dynasty sits on a hilltop above the old city and has become Fez's best panoramic viewpoint, looking down over the whole of Fes el-Bali to the Middle Atlas foothills beyond.
Read more
Open 24/7

Borj Nord hill · Fes El Bali
9 min → Ibn Danan Synagogue
3.Ibn Danan Synagogue
Dated to around 1680 and built by the merchant Mimon Boussidan, this Orthodox synagogue in the Mellah — Fez's historic Jewish quarter — was restored and reopened in 1999, and its painted wooden ark and tiled mikveh survive as one of Morocco's best-preserved pieces of Jewish heritage.

6 min · 3 min → Royal Palace of Fez
4.Royal Palace of Fez
A working royal residence closed to visitors, but its seven monumental brass gates at Place des Alaouites — built 1969–71, framed in zellij tilework and carved cedar — are one of the most photographed sights in Fez and the closest the public gets to Dar al-Makhzen.

Day 4
From Hotel: 14 min · 6 min → Andalusian Mosque
1.Andalusian Mosque
Founded in 859–860 for the Andalusi refugees who settled this side of the river, the mosque's 14-step monumental gateway was built in the 13th century by artisans from Nasrid Granada — carved cedar, sculpted plaster and glazed tile crowned by twin domes.
Read more
Open 24/7
~15 min
Near Bab Guissa · Fes El Bali
22 min · 9 min → Bab Ftouh
2.Bab Ftouh
The "Gate of the Opening" marks the southeastern entrance to Fes el-Bali, opening onto the Andalusian quarter; the current gate dates from the Almohad rebuild of 1212, on a site fortified since the 11th century.
Read more
Open 24/7
~10 min
Bab Ftouh · Fes El Bali
12 min · 5 min → Art Naji Pottery Cooperative
3.Art Naji Pottery Cooperative
A family-run ceramics workshop founded by the Fakhari brothers in 1930, just outside Bab Ftouh, where free guided tours follow every stage of Fez's blue pottery and zellij tile-making — clay thrown on foot-powered wheels, hand-cut tesserae, and wood-fired kilns.

28 min · 11 min → Kasbah Cherarda
4.Kasbah Cherarda
Refurbished as a garrison fortress by Sultan Moulay al-Rashid between 1664 and 1672 on the site of an earlier tribal granary kasbah, its long fortified walls — inscribed with the rest of the Medina of Fez as a UNESCO World Heritage Site — are viewed from outside; the interior now holds a hospital and school.

Local Tastes
Pastilla
Fez's signature dish: warqa pastry wrapped around shredded pigeon or chicken, spiced scrambled egg and almonds, dusted with powdered sugar and cinnamon — a sweet-savory combination the city is famous for perfecting.
Dar Hammad · Le Tarbouche · La Maison Bleue
Bissara
A thick split-pea soup, the peas slow-cooked and mashed by hand, served with olive oil and ground cumin — a breakfast staple sold from stalls in the Al Aachabin food section of the medina.
Al Aachabin food stalls
Harira
A tomato-based soup thickened with lentils and chickpeas and finished with fresh herbs — Morocco's most common soup, served daily across the medina and central to the Ramadan table.
Cafe Clock · Medina Cafe
Food Delivery
Glovo
Foreign number: accepted — the SMS code arrives on most international carriers; Moroccan users also verify via WhatsApp when SMS is slow.
Morocco's largest delivery platform, covering restaurants, groceries and pharmacies with typical delivery inside an hour; medina addresses can confuse the app's location pin, so share a landmark — a gate or square name — with the courier in the order notes.
glovoapp.com
Getting Around
inDrive
Foreign number: accepted — the SMS code arrives on most international carriers, and inDrive is built for cross-border use.
Fez's only working ride-hailing app — Uber and Careem don't cover the city. Riders name their own fare and drivers accept or counter-offer, which takes some getting used to; useful for the trip between the train station and the medina gates, since cars can't enter Fes el-Bali itself.
indrive.com

Morocco's capital, with the Hassan Tower, the Kasbah of the Udayas overlooking the Atlantic, and the Mausoleum of Mohammed V.

Heads Up
Chouara Tannery — No official entrance fee
Leather-shop terraces around Tannery Square let you climb up to view the dye pits for free; a small tip is customary if you don't buy anything.
Al-Qarawiyyin — No interior access
Non-Muslims can't enter the prayer hall; the courtyard is viewed only through the open main gate on Derb Boutouil.

Packing for a Hike
Worth Knowing

The world's largest car-free urban zone shapes everything about a visit

Fes el-Bali has no cars, no scooters, and barely any bicycles — goods still move through the medina on handcarts and mules, exactly as they have for a thousand years. That is why every stop in this guide is measured in walking minutes rather than a mix of walking and driving: a taxi genuinely cannot reach most of these addresses, and the "ride" figure that appears on a few motion rows is the time to loop around the walls to the nearest point a car can stop.

The gate colors at Bab Boujloud are a small piece of urban planning disguised as decoration: blue facing outward toward the new city, green facing inward toward the old one, so a reader can tell at a glance which direction they are walking without needing to check street signs.

The Water Clock at Dar al-Magana and the Bou Inania Madrasa across the street from it were built by the same sultan in the same decade — Abu Inan Faris commissioned both within a few years of each other, which is why the pairing works so well as a single stop-to-stop hop.
